newsitem.title: UK: Smart car -- new way or too small, pricey, ugly?.
newsitem.headline: Smart car -- new way or too small, pricey, ugly?.

text.p: Manufacturers of the tiny Smart car say it is a revolution in the making that will change urban driving for ever.
But detractors see a venture offering a vehicle that is too small, too expensive, and too ugly.

For Lars Brorsen -- chief executive officer of Micro Compact Car AG, which will make Smart -- it is the car of the future. The diminutive two-seater will help solve the problem of urban traffic in a stylish, safe and environmentally friendly way, according to Brorsen.
Analysts are not so sure.

They believe sales projections are wildly optimistic. Smart is to be produced by a 1.5 billion-mark ($868 million) joint venture by German luxury car maker Mercedes and SMH of Switzerland. SMH, the acronym for Suisse Microelectronique et dHorlogerie is better known for making Swatch watches.

Analysts also doubt the concept behind the car. Small cars shortly appearing from mass car makers like Germany's Volkswagen AG and Italy's Fiat SpA will not only undercut the $9,260 base price for Smart, but offer four seats.

Peter Schmidt, analyst at Automotive Industry Data, said most big car companies believe minicars will indeed be a most successful new sector, but the public will not go for something as radical as the Smart.
"All the mainstream manufacturers are trying to produce small, affordable cars for the masses. I think VW will be able to offer a little car for less than $9,000 that seats four," Schmidt said.

"No doubt Mercedes, like everybody else, has identified that this sector will have significant growth. But you have to have the right product. No doubt time will tell, but it is not only incredibly ugly, it only has two seats," he said.

The 600-cubic-centimetre Smart enters production later this year at a factory in Saareguemines, France, and should appear in Europe by March or April. Because of the space limitations of the 8-foot-by-5-foot design -- Smart says three cars sideways will take up the area of a normal parking space -- styling is practical rather than romantic.
The rear of the car drops straight down from just behind the front seats.
"However you look at it, there has to be a huge question mark over its success. I don't know of any other manufacturer that plans to enter that section of the market with a two-seater," Schmidt said.
VW is unveiling its little Lupo at the Frankfurt car show in September, and plans a stripped-down version next year called the Lupino. Schmidt believes even the Lupo will be cheaper than the Smart.

Smart production capacity of 200,000 is unlikely to be met anytime soon. Schmidt believes 100,000 will be tough to reach. Smart has been relentlessly cutting back its sales projections, with Brorsen now expecting 100,000 in 1998.
Smart had predicted 160,000 in 1998, rising to 200,000 by 2000.
Nigel Griffiths, European motor analyst at McGraw-Hill's DRI, believes sales will only reach between 70,000 and 80,000 in 1998, with a long-term maximum of not more than 130,000.
Even a small car specialist like Fiat couldn't sell many more than 150,000 Cinquecentos a year, Griffiths said.
Griffiths said new models from Fiat in this sector next year, and later from a possible General Motors/Suzuki Motor partnership, would provide tough competition.

Japanese companies like Toyota Motor Corp. and Nissan Motor Co Ltd. with experience in the 1.5 million-a-year local minicar market will also be free to attack this sector after European trading barriers disappear by 2000.
Smart's Brorsen is undaunted.
"Our aim is for a car which is value for money," he said.
